description: Joint and segregated conjugal roles, the domestic division of labour, and Oakley's feminist critique.
content_html:
What Are Conjugal Roles?

Conjugal roles refer to the roles performed by each partner within a couple relationship. Sociologists distinguish between two broad patterns. Joint conjugal roles (also called integrated conjugal roles) describe partnerships where tasks, decision making and leisure are shared between partners. Segregated conjugal roles describe partnerships where male and female partners have clearly defined separate tasks — typically, the man in paid employment and the woman in domestic work and child rearing. Understanding how sociologists explain these patterns — and whether they are changing — is a key part of the families topic.

The Domestic Division of Labour

The domestic division of labour refers to how unpaid household tasks and child rearing are distributed within the home. Sociologists study a range of activities: cooking, cleaning, laundry, child care, disciplining children, managing household finances, arranging leisure activities and making major household decisions. The central question is whether this division is equal between partners, and whether it has become more equal over time.

Functionalist View: Complementary Roles

Talcott Parsons argued that the gender-divided conjugal role pattern — the man performing the instrumental role (breadwinner, financial provider) and the woman performing the expressive role (homemaker, emotional carer) — was both naturally grounded and functionally efficient. From this perspective, segregated conjugal roles are complementary: each partner contributes different but equally important tasks, and the division benefits the family as a whole. Parsons presented this pattern as meeting the needs of modern industrial society, where paid employment is geographically mobile and requires one adult to be free to move while the other maintains the home.

Peter Willmott and Michael Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal over time. Their research suggested that the family was moving through historical stages and that the modern family was becoming “symmetrical” — meaning that partners were increasingly sharing domestic tasks and leisure. Willmott and Young described the symmetrical family as one where roles are not identical but broadly equal in the time and effort each partner contributes. They linked this change to the principle of stratified diffusion: lifestyle changes begin among middle-class families and gradually spread to working-class families. For Willmott and Young, the trend towards symmetry was a positive “march of progress” in family life.

Oakley’s Feminist Critique: The Myth of the Symmetrical Family

Ann Oakley directly challenged Willmott and Young’s optimistic picture. Her research on housework, published in The Sociology of Housework (1974), found that the domestic division of labour remained profoundly unequal despite changes in women’s employment. Oakley argued that the conventional family — with its gender-divided roles — was not disappearing but persisting in new forms. She criticised Willmott and Young’s methodology, noting that their data on male domestic participation was based on a very low threshold — men who helped with housework at least once a week counted as “participating.”

Oakley developed the concept of the double shift to describe the burden on women who work in paid employment but continue to perform the majority of domestic labour at home. Rather than replacing domestic work, women’s entry into the paid labour market added a second shift to their day. Some feminist sociologists have extended this to the concept of the triple shift — paid work, domestic labour, and the emotional management of family relationships — to capture the full range of work that women typically carry out.

Key Fact

Willmott and Young (1973) argued that conjugal roles were becoming more equal through the “symmetrical family” and the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley argued this was a myth — her research showed that the domestic division of labour remained unequal and that women performed a “double shift” of paid work and domestic labour.

Contemporary Issues in Conjugal Roles

Sociologists study a range of contemporary issues that affect the division of roles within couples. Decision making — who has the final say on major financial or household decisions — remains gendered in many households, with research suggesting men retain greater power over major financial decisions. Money management patterns vary: in some families one partner controls all finances; in others both have independent access to income. Dual career families — where both partners are in full-time paid employment — have grown significantly, raising questions about how domestic labour is redistributed. Child rearing responsibilities, including who attends medical appointments, manages schooling and provides primary emotional care, continue to fall disproportionately on women in many families. Leisure activities — how much free time each partner has and how it is used — also differ: research consistently shows that men have more free leisure time than women in couples.

Key Fact

Feminist sociologists argue that the domestic division of labour remains unequal in contemporary British families. Women who work full-time still perform more domestic labour and child care than their male partners on average, supporting Oakley’s concept of the double shift.

From a Marxist perspective, the domestic division of labour serves the interests of capitalism as well as men. The unpaid domestic labour of women — cooking, cleaning, child rearing, caring for sick and elderly family members — reproduces the labour force at no cost to employers. This work is economically invisible: it does not appear in GDP or in wage statistics, yet it sustains the workforce. Marxist feminists argue that the conventional family therefore benefits the bourgeoisie as well as individual men, because it means the costs of reproducing workers across generations are borne by families rather than by the state or employers.
exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark Discuss question about conjugal roles, the key is to present the debate between Willmott and Young’s symmetrical family thesis and Oakley’s feminist counter-argument clearly. Name both: “Willmott and Young argued that…” and “Oakley challenged this, arguing that…”. Add the functionalist perspective (Parsons on complementary roles) and the Marxist feminist view (unpaid domestic labour benefits capitalism) to reach the top band. A common mistake on 4-mark Describe questions is describing the domestic division of labour without specifying the activities involved — mention decision making, money management, child rearing and leisure to show breadth. On a 2-mark Define question for “double shift”, make sure you include both components: paid employment AND domestic labour — leaving out one component is worth only 1 mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Conjugal roles describe how partners divide paid work, domestic tasks and child rearing. Joint conjugal roles are relatively equal; segregated conjugal roles assign distinct tasks by gender. The domestic division of labour covers decision making, money management, child rearing, domestic tasks and leisure.
  • Willmott and Young (1973) argued the family was becoming symmetrical through the principle of stratified diffusion. Oakley challenged this as a myth — her research showed the domestic division of labour remained unequal and women performed a double shift of paid work and domestic labour.
  • Parsons (functionalist) saw gender-divided conjugal roles as complementary and beneficial. Marxists argue that women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces the workforce at no cost to capitalism. Feminists (Oakley) argue the conventional family is a patriarchal institution that exploits women's labour.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'segregated conjugal roles'?
A) Both partners share domestic tasks and leisure activities equally
B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour
C) One partner performs all tasks while the other is absent from the household
D) Roles are negotiated week by week depending on work schedules
practice_questions.marks: B) Male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — typically the man in paid work and the woman in domestic labour [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying that it refers to women who work in paid employment; 1 mark for explaining that they also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home. Example: 'The double shift refers to the situation in which women who are in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home, effectively working two shifts in a day.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe Oakley's feminist criticism of Willmott and Young's symmetrical family thesis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying Oakley's criticism (e.g. the symmetrical family is a myth; the domestic division of labour remained unequal). 2 marks for a developed description: e.g. 'Oakley argued that Willmott and Young's methodology was flawed — their measure of male domestic participation was set too low (helping with housework once a week counted as "participating"). Her own research found that women continued to perform the majority of domestic tasks even when in paid employment, creating a double shift of paid work and domestic labour.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the functionalist view of conjugal role relationships within the family.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for identifying the functionalist perspective (Parsons). 1 mark for describing the instrumental role (male breadwinner, financial provider). 1 mark for describing the expressive role (female homemaker and emotional carer). 1 mark for a developed explanation of why Parsons saw this as functional: the division is complementary — each role is distinct but equally important; together they meet the family's and society's needs. Stronger answers note that Parsons saw this as matching the demands of a geographically mobile industrial economy.

practice_questions.text: Describe the principle of stratified diffusion as used by Willmott and Young to explain changes in conjugal role relationships.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 1 mark for naming Willmott and Young. 1 mark for defining the principle of stratified diffusion (lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and spread downwards to the working class over time). 1 mark for linking it to conjugal roles (joint/symmetrical roles develop first in middle-class families and spread to working-class families). 1 mark for a developed explanation or example: e.g. dual career families and shared domestic tasks were first most common among professional middle-class couples and later became more widespread across social classes.

practice_questions.text: "Conjugal role relationships have become equal between men and women in contemporary Britain." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): A sustained argument presenting multiple perspectives. Arguments in favour of growing equality: Willmott and Young's symmetrical family thesis — roles are becoming more equal through stratified diffusion; growth of dual career families; more men taking paternity leave; legal changes promoting gender equality at work. Arguments against: Oakley's feminist critique — the domestic division of labour remains unequal; women perform the double (or triple) shift; decision making and money management continue to favour men. Marxist feminist view — women's unpaid domestic labour continues to benefit capitalism. Parsons's functionalist argument could be noted as endorsing the traditional division but as a descriptive point rather than supporting gender equality. At least two named sociologists developed in detail. Sociological vocabulary (conjugal roles, domestic division of labour, symmetrical family, double shift, patriarchy, stratified diffusion) used accurately. Supported conclusion.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present with named sociologists. Judgement present but uneven development.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant points, mostly one-sided or undeveloped. Some named theorists. Conclusion assertive.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points, mainly description. Few named sociologists. Little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociologist argued in 1973 that the family was becoming 'symmetrical' with roles more equally shared between partners?
Oakley used the term 'double shift' to describe women who perform paid employment AND also continue to perform most of the _____ at home.
Conjugal roles in which both partners share tasks and leisure relatively equally are called _____ conjugal roles.
Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes start among the middle class and spread to the working class is called the principle of _____ diffusion.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: The distribution of unpaid household tasks and child rearing between partners
Oakley's term for a family arrangement in which the woman is the primary homemaker and the man the primary breadwinner
The phenomenon in which women in paid employment also perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour

glossary_terms.definition: The roles and responsibilities performed by partners within a marriage or cohabiting relationship, including paid work, domestic labour and child rearing.
A pattern of conjugal roles in which partners share domestic tasks, paid work and decision making relatively equally; also called integrated conjugal roles.
A pattern of conjugal roles in which male and female partners have distinct, separate tasks — the male typically in paid work, the female in domestic labour.
The distribution of unpaid household tasks and child rearing responsibilities between partners within the home.
The phenomenon in which women who work in paid employment also continue to perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home.
Willmott and Young's term for a family form in which partners share domestic tasks and leisure relatively equally, though not necessarily identically.
Oakley's term for the arrangement in which the woman is the primary homemaker and the man the primary breadwinner, characterised by segregated conjugal roles.
Willmott and Young's argument that lifestyle changes begin among the middle class and gradually spread down to the working class.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the domestic division of labour?
flashcard_questions.a: The distribution of unpaid household tasks and child rearing responsibilities between partners within the home.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the double shift, according to Oakley?
flashcard_questions.a: The situation in which women in paid employment also perform the majority of unpaid domestic labour at home.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Oakley criticise Willmott and Young's research methodology?
flashcard_questions.a: She argued they set the threshold for male participation too low — helping with housework once a week counted as participating.
The male breadwinner role, focused on paid employment and providing financially for the family.
The female nurturing role, focused on the emotional wellbeing of children and management of the home.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do Marxist feminists argue the domestic division of labour benefits capitalism?
flashcard_questions.a: Women's unpaid domestic labour reproduces the workforce at no cost to employers, making it economically invisible but essential.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the conventional family, according to Oakley?
flashcard_questions.a: A family arrangement in which the woman is the primary homemaker and the man the primary breadwinner, with segregated roles.
